rewrites.summary:
A self-governing archipelago in the Realm of Denmark: domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after church-state friction. Nothing in the audited record criminalises trans people or documents enforcement against them.

The climate is measured by politics rather than prosecution: in 2006 activists gathered some 20,000 signatures — a large share of a ~50,000 population — demanding anti-discrimination protection after surveys found violence and discrimination against out gay people 'not uncommon' and legally unaddressed; a Centre Party MP who refused to share a state banquet with Iceland's gay premier (2010, 'a direct provocation') was still demanding Pride bans in 2015, when a nationally beloved singer urged the public to ignore him. For a visitor: low violence risk, thin legal protection, and high-profile political hostility to visibility.

A 2006 petition of ~20,000 signatures against a population near 50,000 demanded anti-discrimination law after surveys found anti-LGBT violence 'not uncommon' and legally unaddressed. A centrist politician refused protocol contact with a neighbouring state's gay head of government (2010) and later demanded Pride bans (2015), drawing rebuke from prominent artists. No enforcement against trans people is documented; visibility invites documented political hostility.

rewrites.summary:
A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.

For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010 and a national equality association (Qaamaneq, 2014). The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: some 56,000 people across remote settlements means thin institutional reach, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.
rewrites.blindSummary: The world's largest island, self-governing within a European kingdom's realm, with its own parliament and courts for domestic matters. Partnership law arrived from the metropolitan framework in 1996 with almost no debate; marriage equality followed in 2016, passed unanimously locally with church support; gender recognition adopted self-declaration the same year, earlier than the metropolitan state's own practice. Reporting describes gay life as quiet, integrated and non-violent, with a small Pride and a national association founded 2014. Sparse population and remote settlements mean thin capacity; documented risk is capacity, not hostility.

rewrites.summary:
A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.
rewrites.blindSummary: A Caribbean island territory of a large federal republic whose nationals it holds: federal identification and airport-screening rules apply with no local offset. In July 2025 the territory enacted its own ban on gender-affirming care for people under 21 — the federal state's severest, with felony penalties, fines and licence loss for providers and potential exposure for consenting parents; litigation was announced; the signatory had courted LGBT voters. Local history is mixed: marriage equality came via the federal courts after local plaintiffs sued (2014); conversion-therapy and religious-freedom bills advanced (2019) then were withdrawn under pressure. Visitor exposure combines federal paperwork friction with locally criminalised care provision.

Policy news (Apr 2019): activists criticised religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills in the territory's legislature.
Policy news (June 2014): four same-sex couples joined the suit against the territory's marriage ban.
Policy news (Mar 2019): lawmakers blocked a vote on banning conversion therapy for minors.
Policy news (June 2019): the governor ordered withdrawal of those bills, a point for advocates.
Political newsletter (July 2025): the territory enacted the federal state's most extreme care ban — criminal penalties to under-21s even with consent, court challenges announced.

rewrites.summary:
An unincorporated US territory, so the 2025–26 federal turn — marker/document policy, TSA screening, the trans military-exclusion order — lands hard on an island whose economy and society carry a large permanent US military presence. Local law partly cuts the other way: Guam was the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, after a local lesbian couple sued over a denied licence), its statute book bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage has applied since 2009.

Academic Pacific-identity surveys record indigenous Chamorro understandings of gender diversity, and a local advocacy scene maintains ID-documents guidance for residents. The synthesis for a visitor: real written protections and a quiet, integrated public record, against military-community conservatism, federal volatility amplified by the base, and small-island visibility where an outed stranger is noticed.
rewrites.blindSummary: A Western Pacific island territory of a large federal republic: federal documents and screening policy apply, and federal military policy restricting trans service members has outsized local weight due to a permanent stationed force. The territory was its federal state's first to recognise same-sex marriage (2015, following a local couple's lawsuit). Local statute bars employment discrimination including gender identity, and federal hate-crime coverage applies; academic surveys record indigenous gender-diversity traditions; residents run practical ID-change guidance. Reporting describes a quiet, integrated presence; countervailing forces are military-community conservatism, federal volatility and small-population visibility.

rewrites.summary:
A small US territory: federal document and airport policy applies, and the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through it (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it. Locally the record is quietly protective rather than hostile: the Attorney General ruled in 2017 that the human-rights law's sex provision covers transgender students — an official extension of territorial protection — and local media framed the community's position after the 2016 federal shock as 'losses... but reason for hope.'

No criminalisation, documented anti-trans enforcement or care ban appears in the audited record; equally, protection rests on an attorney-general's interpretation rather than legislation, and the islands' scale (tens of thousands across three main islands) means high everyday recognition risk. Federal rollback above, a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture beneath.
rewrites.blindSummary: A small Caribbean island territory of a large federal republic: federal identification and screening policy applies in full, including post-2025 marker restrictions. No criminal prohibitions and no care bans. Law officers have ruled (2017) that the territorial human-rights statute's sex provision covers transgender students — administrative interpretation, not codification. Local reporting saw setbacks and cautious hope after the 2016 federal election. Small population means anonymity is hard; documented local posture is protective, federal framework restrictive.

rewrites.summary:
A US territory governed partly through chiefly custom (fa'a matai). Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the modern code (decriminalised in the early 1980s; no audited source documents any enforcement since), but American Samoa was long the one US territory where federal marriage equality did not plainly apply — the attorney general said in 2015 it was 'still being reviewed' while every other territory adopted it, and the local constitution defines marriage traditionally. As US nationals, residents and visitors carry the 2025–26 federal document and screening friction, with no local non-discrimination shield of substance.

The Pacific academic record documents fa'afafine — a long-standing third-gender presence in Samoan family life — while contemporaneous travel advice describes a traditional, church-centred society where custom sets conformity. For an outed trans visitor: no criminal law, minimal institutional protection, unresolved questions about which federal guarantees reach the islands, and communal rather than state pressure.
rewrites.blindSummary: A South Pacific island territory of a large federal republic under customary chiefly structures alongside elected ones. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised (early-1980s decriminalisation; no enforcement documented), but the territory stood apart from the federal marriage-equality settlement — officials said in 2015 the federal ruling was 'still under review' while sister territories adopted it, and the constitution defines marriage traditionally. Federal document and screening rules apply to US nationals. Academic surveys record an indigenous third-gender presence; travel writing describes church-and-custom conformity. Institutional protection is minimal; risk is social, and the reach of federal rights guarantees is unresolved.

rewrites.summary:
A US commonwealth in political union: federal document, immigration and screening policy applies (including 2025–26 marker restrictions), while marriage recognition reached Saipan in 2015 by operation of the federal constitution — recognition exists, and nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression. In 2023 the legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute whose sentencing criteria expressly cover sexual orientation and gender identity — a formal, if recent, protection.

The policy accounting is nonetheless near-bottom: a comprehensive US equality index scores the commonwealth's gender-identity law in negative territory (sexual-orientation law 'low'), citing family-law gaps — no second-parent adoption, no assisted-reproduction recognition, no family-services protection. Visitor reality: no documented legal danger, a fresh hate-crime shield, minimal other institutional support, and high social visibility in small, church-influenced islands.
rewrites.blindSummary: A Western Pacific island commonwealth in political union with a large federal republic: federal documents and screening rules apply in full. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised and marriage recognition arrived in 2015 via the federal constitution. In 2023 the local legislature enacted a hate-crimes statute expressly covering sexual orientation and gender identity. Beyond that, comparative policy audits place its LGBT law near the federal state's bottom: no general non-discrimination codification, adoption and assisted-reproduction gaps. Customary and religious structures raise everyday visibility in small populations.

rewrites.summary:
A self-governing island state in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands criminalised male same-sex acts under a 1969 colonial-era Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023 — after a decade of stalled bills, NZ-assisted drafting, and sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the laws 'draconian' colonial relics. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent; the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation. Post-decriminalisation there is still no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; public life is strongly church-inflected; the islands are some 15,000 people where everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.
rewrites.blindSummary: A small self-governing island state in free association with a larger Oceanian partner to the south. Its criminal code carried colonial-era provisions punishing male same-sex acts (up to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until a 2023 repeal, after a decade of stalled bills and sustained local advocacy with the partner state's drafting help; enforcement in living memory was undocumented, so the repeal lifted a latent risk. Historical reporting frames pre-colonial acceptance of same-sex relationships, disrupted by colonisation. Church-inflected public culture; marriage equality and general non-discrimination protections remain absent in a very small, mutually known population.

International rights news (Oct 2020): the bill stalled again; penalties stood at seven years; comment notes pre-colonial acceptance.
International rights news (Aug 2017): draft crimes code (partner-drafted) to remove sections with 7- and 5-year penalties; local association called them draconian relics.
Partner public radio (Aug 2017): parliament opened submissions on the replacement crimes bill; the LGBTI association filed in support.
rewrites.notes: 'Still criminalises' flag reversed by sourced 2023 repeal; church framing via 2020 claim.

rewrites.summary:
One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.
rewrites.blindSummary: One of the world's smallest island states, self-governing in free association with a larger Oceanian partner. Inherited colonial offences were removed (consent reportedly equalised 2011) and no enforcement against queer people is documented; but there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination protection, and uneven ages of majority appear on the principal act's face. UN regional documentation lists the indigenous third-gender role as cultural heritage — deep family acceptance alongside church-driven conservatism. Legacy law permits HIV testing of long-stay visitors. Under two thousand residents makes anonymity impossible; risk is social, undocumented in both directions.
blindSourceSummaries: Legal-watchdog overview of colonial-era criminalisation across the region: this state carries no such offences.
UN campaign Pacific fact sheet (2015): lists the indigenous third-gender role as part of regional cultural heritage.

Independent legal-reference page: uneven statutory ages of majority under the principal act; consent equalised c.2011; no relationship recognition; visitor HIV-testing provisions for stays over two months.

rewrites.summary:
A special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement: trans claims here have been fought in court more than legislated. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the apex court in 2023 ruled full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — reversing a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation. Beyond the card, however, recognition still runs on surgery; and where the executive has chosen, it has chosen against: in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, so relationship recognition and any SOGI equality ordinance remain absent.

Corporate visibility invites backlash (a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016), and open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law. Visitor arithmetic: no criminal law, dense urban anonymity, a functioning marker-change route on cards — inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and whose politicians recently voted inclusion down.
rewrites.blindSummary: A dense East Asian financial city with its own separate legal system under a constitutional document within a one-party great power. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised; the top court in 2023 barred surgery as a precondition for gender-marker changes on compulsory identity documents, reversing a 2019 loss — though surgery conditions still govern other recognition routes. The legislature rejected the executive's own partnership bill (71–14, Sept 2025) after judicial deadlines; there is no relationship recognition or equality ordinance. Corporate LGBT visibility has draws organised backlash, and open activism operates in a climate tightened since 2020 security legislation. Visitor-facing: no criminal risk, real card route, dense anonymity, absent legislative protection.

Rights news (Feb 2019): high court rejected three trans men's bid for marker change without surgery; judge called surgery the only objective criterion.
Independent local daily (Dec 2016): a bank's rainbow installations and the homophobic backlash — climate around corporate visibility.
Court-of-appeal archive (2006): equal-consent litigation examining discriminatory offences — a foundational precedent.

rewrites.summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.
rewrites.blindSummary: A compact southern city that is a Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of European derivation: its code criminalises neither same-sex conduct nor gender expression, and offers no legal gender recognition, no relationship recognition and no non-discrimination protection. A 2015 advocacy meeting on ID-marker changes proceeded behind a screen; the 2016 domestic-violence law deliberately excluded same-sex partners from protection despite a UN treaty-body direction, a choice civil society publicly condemned as state-endorsed discrimination. Officials treat the topic as a non-issue: total absence of legal risk and near-total absence of recourse, with high social familiarity.

rewrites.summary:
A disputed North African territory under military administration by a neighbouring state, whose penal code governs any visitor: same-sex intimacy is criminalised (six months to three years) with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people — rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition (a 2021 path covers intersex people only); the administering state's religious establishment has condemned transition.

Occupation stacks the risk: 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign, rights defenders tried at the territory's own court (a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark), and a 2018 legal study recording LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike. For an outed visitor: criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.
rewrites.blindSummary: A disputed territory under military administration by a neighbouring state; that state's penal code applies: same-sex acts criminalised (six months to three years) with arbitrary enforcement, morality provisions used against gender-nonconforming people at document counters and checkpoints, no gender-affirming healthcare, no legal gender recognition for trans people (an intersex-only path exists), and the administering state's religious authority opposes transition. Occupation adds politically charged trials, a documented organised outing campaign, and reporting of LGBTI residents exposed to violations by state and non-state actors with no civil space. Large charge volumes regionally; negligible local recourse.
